claims.text: Above 900 °C, a sufficient concentration of Si, Mn, or Al in CrFeCoNiX drives preferential formation of a continuous, coherent oxide.
The protective oxide may be a spinel, alumina, or silica-based phase.
Selective oxidation kinetics of X, interfacial diffusion, and thermal-expansion compatibility with the substrate govern scale stability.
A favorable balance of oxidation, diffusion, and thermal expansion produces a self-healing, adherent scale that resists cracking and spallation.
The relevant starting material can be either a single-phase or multiphase metallic solid solution.
The continuously grown adherent surface oxide originates from selective oxidation of element X.
Element X oxidizes preferentially because it has a higher chemical potential than the other alloy constituents.
A critical threshold concentration or activity of X is required for protective-scale formation.
Above the critical X threshold, the resulting oxide has sufficient thermodynamic stability and appropriate diffusion kinetics to remain compatible with substrate thermal expansion.
Insufficient X activity or imbalanced diffusion kinetics causes heterogeneous oxide formation followed by cracking or spallation.
Alloys containing an optimum amount of X will retain a stable, coherent protective scale during high-temperature exposure.
X-deficient alloys or alloys with unfavorable diffusion kinetics will form unstable oxide layers that crack or spall.
A comparable CrFeCoNi alloy with lower or non-optimized X content will produce a less coherent oxide scale under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed behavior applies above 900 °C in oxygen-rich or corrosive atmospheres.
Oxygen partial pressure and additional corrosive species can alter oxide stability.
Failure of higher-X samples to outperform lower-X samples in scale coherence and integrity would falsify the hypothesis.
